name: Morning sunlight viewing

card.summary: Spending time outdoors soon after waking to anchor the body clock; related to established light-therapy research, with no appearance studies.
card.note: Looking directly at the sun can harm eyes.

quick.overview:
Morning sunlight viewing is the practice of spending roughly ten to thirty minutes outdoors after waking, on the idea that early light sets the circadian clock and so supports sleep and general well-being.

The underlying idea of timed light exposure is studied in bright light therapy, where morning treatment is used for seasonal depression and circadian sleep disorders. No study has tested the outdoor practice for appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Light acts on specialised retinal cells that reset the body's internal clock and suppress melatonin. The effect depends on timing relative to the body's core temperature minimum.
quick.risks: Intense light of any kind can harm eyes and skin, and unprotected UV exposure raises skin cancer risk. Light therapy can trigger mania in susceptible people.

lead: Morning sunlight viewing is a lifestyle practice in which people spend roughly ten to thirty minutes outside soon after waking, with the stated aim of anchoring the circadian clock.

The general principle that light resets the body's internal clock is established in light therapy. Wikipedia reports that light suppresses melatonin through light-sensitive retinal cells and that morning treatment has worked best for seasonal affective disorder because early light helps set the circadian rhythm [1].
No studies were found testing the outdoor practice itself for appearance outcomes.

paras: Bright light therapy uses bright visible light, mainly for seasonal affective disorder and circadian sleep-wake disorders such as delayed sleep phase disorder, non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder, shift work and jet lag. Light boxes can emit up to 10,000 lux at a set distance, and the effect depends on timing relative to the body's core temperature minimum [1].

Reported side effects of light therapy include jitteriness, headache, eye irritation, nausea, and triggering of mania or anxiety. Ultraviolet exposure damages skin and is linked to skin cancer and cataracts, and the American Academy of Ophthalmology reports no evidence that blue-light devices damage eyes [1].

No studies found on morning outdoor sunlight viewing for appearance outcomes. Controlled research on timed light exposure comes from bright light therapy, which has shown reduced depressive symptoms in seasonal affective disorder, with mixed or limited evidence in other conditions [1].
